newsitem.title: USA: Sears profits up, stock off on credit card woes.
newsitem.headline: Sears profits up, stock off on credit card woes.

text.p: The U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts filed a civil complaint against Sears, Roebuck & Co. Thursday to stop allegedly "fraudulent" debt collection activities, dealing a blow to the retailer as it reported solid first-quarter results.
U.S. Attorney Donald Stern also said a federal investigation into Sears' practice of collecting debts from its once-bankrupt credit card customers was continuing.

As a matter of company policy, Sears misled many of its indebted credit card holders into believing they had to pay their bills, even though those debts had been nullified by a bankruptcy court, according to court papers.

The announcements highlight Sears' questionable handling in recent years of debts owed by bankrupt credit card holders, raising uncertainty about the second-largest U.S. retailer's exposure to potential legal costs.

Sears said it remains unable to estimate the potential costs of the problem. "No provision has been recorded for it in the first quarter, although it may be material to 1997 operating results," Sears said Thursday.

The latest embarrassment occurred as Sears said first-quarter earnings jumped more than 20 percent, thanks to gains in sales of women's sportswear and dresses, children's apparel and footwear. Lawn tractors and mowers also sold briskly as customers prepared for spring, Sears said.

The Hoffman Estates, Ill.-based retailer said its earnings rose to $182 million in the first quarter from $151 million in the year-ago period. Earnings per share rose to 46 cents from 36 cents, beating analysts' consensus estimate of about 43 cents. Revenues rose to $8.76 billion from $7.99 billion.

"In the merchandising end of the business ... they got a nice improvement in the gross margin and costs were well controlled," said Joseph Ronning, retail analyst at the Brown Brothers Harriman brokerage and investment bank in New York.

However, Sears' stock fell $2 to $46.75 on the New York Stock Exchange as the company's debt problems and complaints about its allegedly "fradulent" debt collection activities overshadowed its strong quarterly results.
Sears reported that its U.S. provision for uncollectible charge accounts rose 18.9 percent to $269 million in the first quarter from $227 million a year ago.

"The increase in account charge-offs reflects the continuation of an industry-wide increase in personal bankruptcies and delinquencies, as well as growth in the credit receivable portfolio," Sears said.
The rising bad debt rate continues a trend that began last year, analysts said.

"If there's a concern, I think it lies in credit," said Judy Meehan, a retail analyst at Parker/Hunter Inc., a brokerage and investment firm in Pittsburgh. "Not just at Sears, but all across the industry, we're seeing increasing delinquency rates and bankruptcies."
U.S. Attorney Stern's office alleged that Sears conducted an "intentional and deliberate practice" to obtain agreements, called reaffirmations, to collect debts.

"In obtaining these agreements, Sears deceived debtors into thinking that they were obligated to pay back debts which had already been discharged by the bankruptcy court," Stern said in a press release.

The company earlier this month admitted that it exercised "flawed legal judgment" and would refund tens of millions of dollars it collected from bankrupt credit card holders around the country, which could cost it tens of millions of dollars.
The collections were made in some cases after Sears reached so-called reaffirmation agreements with bankrupt card holders.

U.S. Bankruptcy Court Judge Carol Kenner in Boston said Wednesday that Sears misled some of its bankrupt card holders into believing they had to repay debts to the company, even though their bills had been nullified by the bankruptcy court.

The retailer said it had reached about $400 million in reaffirmation agreements with card holders around the country between 1992 and early 1997. It remains unknown how many of those agreements were improper, analysts said.
In Massachusetts alone, Sears has admitted to collecting from at least 2,733 such debtors, Stern's office said.
Sears had previously trumpeted to financial analysts its ability to reach such reaffirmation agreements.

Sears reiterated Thursday that it has filed a voluntary nationwide restitution plan regarding the matter. The company said it also was aware that related lawsuits by groups of card holders and Sears shareholders have been filed.
